CHARGES BY HON. G. N. GORDON
speechtext:
I have
been asked by the chairman of the committee investigating the charges made by Hon. G. N.
Gordon to present the second report of the special committee appointed to inquire into certain charges and allegations made by Hon. G. N. Gordon, K.C., together with the exhibits filed, and a copy of the proceedings and evidence taken:
The special committee appointed to inquire into certain charges and allegations made by the Hon. George N. Gordon, K.C., beg leave to present the following as a second report:
After hearing the evidence, your committee is agreed that the charges and allegations contained in the extracts from The Globe newspaper, as set out in the order of reference, were, in fact, made upon public occasions in Hamilton, Ont., on January 6, 1932, and in Lindsay, Ont., on January 8, 1932, by the Hon. George N. Gordon, K.C., as reported in The Globe newspaper of Toronto, Ont., with the exception that the words "Mrs. Herridge" appear in The Globe of January 6, whereas the words "Mr. Herridge" were those used.
As to the statement that a new private car was constructed for the use of the Prime Minister at a cost to the people of Canada of $125,000, your committee feels that this charge is of a relatively minor character, it being a charge of extravagant expenditure, and not one of misappropriation. It finds, however, that the statements made in this respect gave an entirely erroneous impression of the transaction, and were not warranted by the facts as brought out in evidence. Your committee points out that there has been no increase in the number of government private cars since the present government assumed office.
As to the charges and allegations so made, other than that above dealt with, your committee is of the opinion that they were of a most serious nature, calculated to do injury to the reputation of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. Prime Minister of Canada, a member of the House of Commons; and your committee finds that the charges and allegations so made were untrue.
Your committee finds further that these charges and allegations were made with the intention of injuring the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. Prime Minister of Canada, a member of the House of Commons, in his office as Prime Minister, and were made recklessly and without any adequate attempt to ascertain, before making them, whether they were true or untrue.
In the opinion of your committee, the conduct of Mr. Gordon in making the statements he did was reprehensible and deserving of the censure of the House of Commons, the more so as Mr. Gordon is a member of the King's Privy Council for the Dominion of Canada.
A copy of the proceedings and evidence taken, together with the exhibits filed, is attached.
All of whioh is respectfully submitted.
G. R. Geary,
Chairman.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST BY CITY OF PRINCE RUPERT FOR FEDERAL AID
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the government based on a telegram which I received this morning from the city of Prince Rupert. It is as follows:
At a meeting of the council held on the fourteenth instant the following resolution was passed and I was instructed to telegraph the same to you:
"Whereas the city of Prince Rupert has carried the burden of feeding the destitute at a cost beyond the capacity of the city to carry, and whereas the number of these destitute will probably be doubled on account of the halibut fishing being already deemed a failure in this port, the halibut prices down to three and a half cents and two cents making it impossible for fishermen to carry on, and whereas the fishing industry is the only payroll at present possible in this city, and whereas the destitute are badly in need of clothing as well as of food, and whereas the mining and lumbering industries are completely paralyzed with all mills closed down, and whereas this city is unable to finance the unemployed any further, being also unable to meet their own obligations on account of the reluctance of the bank to help, be it resolved that a wire be sent to both the members of the Dominion and provincial parliaments asking that the Dominion government take over the full charge of the direct relief and that ample provision be made to relieve the acute situation at present existing."
Will the government give this matter serious consideration and speedy action?

Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.

Mr. Speaker, impressed as I am with the significance of this particular occasion and realizing this is the only opportunity I shall have during my forty minutes to say something with which every hon. member in this house will agree, may I as a Scottish born Canadian be permitted to say how much we appreciate the marvellous contribution that has been made to the development and upbuilding of our Canadian nation, both in settlement and in government, by those of Irish birth and lineage.
Hear, hear.
Say it over again.

St. Patrick's Day in
the morning.

Fifteen
hundred years ago that marvellous patron saint of Old Erin landed upon the Irish shores. The spirit and genius of the Irish race, to my mind, has been exemplified in those wonderful lines of the Irish poet O'Shaughnessy:
We are the music makers,
And we are the dreamers of dreams Sitting by lone sea-breakers And sighing by desolate streams.
World losers and world forsakers,
And when the pale moon gleams We are the movers and shakers Of the world forever, it seems.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, with the unanimous consent of the house, you will not take this time off my forty minutes.

Carry on like that,
and we will not.

The real sentiment I desire to express in all sincerity is that we, representing the various portions of the Canadian nation in this house of parliament, express a sincere hope for the prosperity of Erin and that those people of Irish descent, may in years to come be privileged to make an ever increasing contribution to the literature, the music, the arts, the trade, the commerce and the general upbuilding of our Canadian nation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the buttons are off the foils. The resolution before the house has been debated for about ten days.

Too long.

Yes, too long, but due to a deliberate lack of preparation by the government which you support. The resolution to my mind invites consideration under three main heads. In the first place, it is the only announcement we have had during the present session of any government policy to deal with the grave question of unemployment; in the second place, it is indicative of the superlative ineptitude of the administration in its failure to produce at this session a real constructive and comprehensive policy in regard to unemployment; in the third place, it is a blunt and blatant evasion of the ordinary rules of parliamentary procedure, and a ruthless, arrogant and autocratic disregard of the functions and responsibilities of parliament and of the rights of the Canadian people. This resolution entails first, consideration of the record of the administration in dealing with unemployment. I am sorry the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is not in his seat, because he is the arch-author of our present miseries in regard to unemployment.
Oh, oh.
Is there any hon. gentleman opposite, Mr. Speaker, who will deny the scope, the extent and the character of the promises made by the Prime Minister during the election of 1930?
The same old story.
The same old story 1 I suppose my hon. friend wants something new. Well, I am reminded of the song: "Every Little Girl Can Teach You Something New."
Oh, oh.

I trust, Mr. Speaker, that I have a meticulous timekeeper who will take off from my precious forty minutes all these senseless, useless interruptions. I know my hon. friends opposite are restless and apprehensive lest I place again on the pages of Hansard the character and extent of the reckless promises that were made by their leader in 1930.
Turn on the gas.
Order.

Let me tell hon. gentlemen opposite, we shall place those reckless promises on Hansard as frequently as we wish, and we shall go on every platform throughout the dominion and place those extravagant promises before the

Canadian nation. I want hon. gentlemen opposite to explain what their leader meant when he promised the Canadian people: I will cure unemployment. "There is no excuse for unemployment if the government does its duty" in British Columbia; "there is no excuse for hard times if the federal government does its duty!" These promises were either true or *false. If they were true during the summer of 1930, when in the classic language of Sir Henry Drayton, "The sun is still shining and the rivers are still sparkling down to the sea," then they were equally true in 1932. If we are to accept as true the words of the Prime Minister, that there was no excuse for unemployment in Canada during 1930, then those words are a ringing challenge to him in regard to his confessed failure to cure unemployment in 1932. We say these promises were definite, we say they were sweeping, we say they regarded the unemployment problem as a national problem. Let me quote very briefly from the statement made by the right hon. gentleman at Montreal:
Unemployment has become a national problem in Canada. It is the direct result of nine years of unsound economic policies applied by the Liberals.
Hear, hear.
Order.

Surely,
Mr. Speaker, "The Lord hath delivered them into my hands." In 1930 unemployment in Canada, according to Tory speakers, was caused by what? They said it was caused by the policies of the administration of that day. In 1932 we have witnessed the sorry spectacle during this session of member after member of a servile and subservient majority rising in their places and saying: "Oh, world conditions alone are responsible for unemployment in the dominion." Well, Mr. Speaker, they cannot have it both ways. We say that world conditions were responsible for unemployment in 1930 and that world conditions are largely responsible for the deplorable situation in 1932. But we say further that the effect of world conditions upon unemployment in Canada in 1932 has been aggravated and accentuated by the hopeless and futile policies pursued by hon. gentlemen opposite. We say categorically that the promises made have not been kept, and that the Prime Minister has broken faith with the Canadian nation.
No, no.

I say he has most deliberately broken faith with the Canadian nation.

Unemployment Continuance Act
No, no.

Did he, or did he not, tell the Canadian people, "I will end unemployment or perish in the
attempt?"
Didn't he try?
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that he has not ended unemployment.
He has not perished yet.

He is
perishing very, very rapidly, he is disintegrating most perceptibly. According to his own figures produced before this house, on September 19, 1930, there were unemployed in the dominion 117,000. According to the figures given last week by the president of the Trades and Labour Congress to-day there are 550,000 Canadian citizens out of work. So that the concrete result of the policies and the plans of this administration is that we have expended $150,000,000 in eighteen months and have multiplied our unemployed almost fivefold. That is, at the present rate the government are pursuing their policy in regard to unemployment they are expending $100,000,000 a year. With what result? Today we have hunger marchers parading through the streets of Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton, Winnipeg and Montreal. What conditions have we to-day on the spacious plains of our great prairie provinces? What conditions have we on the farms in old Ontario? Yet do we not remember, Mr. Speaker, another voice calling in the far west: "When did free trade fight for you? I will make tariffs fight for you?" But what have their precious, priceless tariffs done for our primary producers and our manufacturers? They have ruined Canadian trade.
No.

I maintain they have ruined Canadian trade. Our trade is down by nearly $1,000,000,000. The government have stifled Canadian trade with their pernicious prohibitions. They have shaken the foundations of imperial trade. What have hon. gentlemen opposite done in regard to agriculture? We have heard our friends from the west, men who have toiled upon the farms and know whereof they speak, state that never since confederation have the prices received by the primary producers been so low as they are to-day under this great fabric of tariffs. "I will make tariffs fight for you."
Why don't you go outside?

Let my hon. friends opposite go out into the constituencies, let them face the people of Canada and ascertain what they think with regard to what the tariff policy of this administration has done for Canadian trade. What has it done? It ruined the New Zealand trade. We have not yet had the New Zealand treaty produced for the consideration of this house, but we have had the spectacle of my very good friend and esteemed opponent, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), sailing to the sunny strands of Waikiki and there endeavouring to repair the ravages that he and his party made in our trade with New Zealand. Then, Mr. Speaker, we had the special session of 1930.
Oh, oh.

You
should be patient and listen to the truth for once. We had the special session of 1930, ostensibly called to redeem the pledge to end unemployment, and what happened during that session? We had increases in two hundred items of the Canadian tariff, and towards the end of that two weeks' session we had thrown in our faces an unemployment policy giving $20,000,000 for purposes only specified in a general and not in a particular way. Any time we dared raise our wicked voices on this side of the house hon. gentlemen opposite said, "Hush, hush; be careful lest ye keep from the councils of the Imperial conference that great Canadian statesman, the Prime Minister."
Foolishly, sir, we permitted him to go to the conference, and what happened? May I draw a contrast for the benefit of the house, and particularly for my hon. friends from the old province of Quebec. You will remember that Sir Louis Davies moved the resolution in 1893 in this commons with regard to preferences; you will remember that after the election of 1896, when Laurier and Fielding were returned to power, a special session was called in April, 1897, on the eve of an imperial conference. They brought down preferences to Great Britain and, after a special session lasting two or three weeks, Laurier sailed for the old land. He laid upon the knees of Queen Victoria the Good, in the year of her diamond jubilee, a magnificent gesture by Canada looking to real imperial unity, not a unity achieved by blustering bargaining such as we see to-day. Laurier returned to Canada after receiving the acclaim of England and
1198	COMMONS

France, and for many months after his return Canada knew not the meaning of political parties.
What happened in 1930? The Prime Minister of Canada, after raising the tariffs against our kith and kin in the motherland, crossed the seas to that lovely old island and strutted most magnificently into the council room of empire, bearing pompously upon his shoulders the newly acquired mandate of public approval. He most imperiously issued to the almost affrighted delegates from the other portions of the empire his ultimatum in regard to a ten per cent increase in tariffs all round and returned to Canada without acclaim or approval. That is the contrast between 1930 and 1897.
Now let us come to the special session. At page 140 of Hansard for that session the Prime Minister said:
. . . we are asking this parliament by the measure now before it first of all to recognize the situation as one of a national character and secondly to agree to the appropriation of the sum of $20,000,000 . . .
Then he stated the various ways in which that money was to be applied. At that time the Prime Minister gave the number of unemployed as 117,000. May I recall the prophetic utterances of my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) on that occasion, as found at page 115 of Hansard for that session:
This proposal to take $20,000,000 of the taxpayers' money and spend it on public works and other things to relieve unemployment is fundamentally unsound. It will not relieve unemployment. It will not relieve the smallest fraction of unemployment. After you have done all this work, you will find more unemployment in the country than you had in the beginning.
Surely that statement has been borne out by the facts. Now I would recall our attitude on that occasion, as indicated by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) at page 163 of Hansard for the second session of 1930:
... I think that would have been entirely the best plan for the government to have adopted-to have appointed a special body for the purpose of administering this fund, to have made that body responsible for every dollar of the expenditure, and to have had the accounts audited in detail by the Auditor General of this country. If that course is not to be followed-and I assume it is not-then I think it is doubly important that great care should be taken to see that the money goes to the destination for which it is intended.
Now I should like to quote, with particular emphasis, the words of the Prime Minister as they appear at page 175 of Hansard for that year:

... I have said further that this government accepts the responsibility that is involved in this expenditure.
What have we to-day in British Columbia? Sitting in the capital city of that province we have a committee investigating the maladministration of unemployment moneys throughout the province, though on the declaration of the Prime Minister himself, as found at page 175 of Hansard, this government has accepted full responsibility for the administration of every cent voted by this parliament in regard to relief in the province of British Columbia. Now may I recall with diffidence my own words on that occasion, as found at page 179 of Hansard. They were almost prophetic also in regard to what was to transpire:
. . . the people of British Columbia to-day do not want the hon. Minister of Finance of British Columbia to be responsible for any expenditure in that province of any part of the money which this parliament is about to vote. . . the people of British Columbia to-day would much prefer to have the expenditure of any portion of this $20,000,000 in the province under the direct supervision of this government . . .
I want to tell hon. gentlemen opposite that if that plan had been followed they would have avoided a great deal of grief in British Columbia. On that occasion we asked four things. We asked the government to bring in a supply bill; we asked that this House of Commons retain control over expenditure; we asked a thorough and complete audit by the Auditor General of this dominion-and this afternoon I am asking this government, through the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), to have a complete audit made of the funds in British Columbia under the auspices of the Auditor General of Canada-and we asked also for the appointment of a national un-emplojmient relief commission.
Now, sir, we come to the session of 1931, and what happened? We had this nefarious bill introduced. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) said the other day that the bill was absolutely in order because it was approved by the Canadian parliament. I want to inform my hon. friend that such approval was only obtained by coercion as far as thfe minority in this parliament was concerned; that bill never did and never will receive the approval of those who believe in the fundamental and essential principles of liberty and the freedom of parliament under the constitution. That bill was divided into three parts. In the first place it dealt with the relief of unemployment in a general way; in the second place it dealt [DOT]vith farm relief in the west, and in the third

place it contained this pernicious phraseology having to do with peace, order and good government in the Dominion of Canada. Canadians take a pride in their history and have a high respect for the constitution which governs them. Its political evolution was slow but those who sacrificed all their talents and even their life to conquer our constitutional liberties, have inculcated in all an unshakable love for these rights so eagerly claimed and honourably obtained from England.
In the Quebec Act, in 1774, it was deemed useless to establish an assembly notwithstanding the earnest pleadings which Fox made in England in favour of a representative assembly.
The Constitutional Act of 1791 divided the country in Upper and Lower Canada. Pitt, the eminent British statesman, though he had reestablished peace, and John Graves Simcoe contended that he had given this country a constitution similar to that of England. Then came the period under which Canada really attained its aim, that is, the union of the two Canadas. Previous to this period, the worthy members who were the true representatives of the Canadian nation, such as William Lyon Mackenzie, Robert Fleming Gourley, Doctor Rolph, Peter Perry, Ketchum, Bidwell, Robert Baldwin and others, in Ontario, as well as Papineau, Nelson, Cuthbert, Lafontaine, Morin, Aylwin and Yiger in Quebec, had struggled hard and united their efforts to attain this end. The situation which existed previous to this period, recurs to-day, and if the Liberal party, faced with the resolution which it is asked to adopt, takes an attitude which displeases our friends opposite, it is that the Liberal party to-day, in keeping faith with the high ideals of the Liberal party of those days, wishes to assert that it will always remain the ardent champion of the people's constitutional liberties.
To ignore the past under the plea of an extraordinary emergency would be to take a step backwards and proclaim ourselves partisans of an anti-national modernism. I consider that unemployment could be somewhat

relieved without exacting that parliament should sacrifice its rights, the surrender of which would be judged by the people severely when the great day of atonement came.
Let us not forget, sir, that we have to face a world-wide crisis and let us endeavour to establish some reforms. The hon. member who preceded me stated that he had not yet heard on the Liberal side any criticism which might bear results; I wish to make one suggestion of a constructive order, by pointing out what the state and industries, at large, might do to improve this chronic unemployment problem from which we suffer.
Anxious to find an antidote against unemployment, the governments were finally affected themselves by this hysterical fit of unemployment relief. We must acknowledge it was to obey a generous impulse that direct assistance, etc., to the unemployed was given, however, by that means only temporary relief was afforded and to a very small number of them. Let us admit, moreover, that these repeated assaults on the treasury would result in further disturbing the equilibrium which should exist between production and distribution, and would in the near future contribute to increase the cost of production and the prices which the public have to pay. Hoarding up, failures, unemployment or deficits are not, properly speaking, the causes of the present crisis, but rather the symptoms of an economic disease resulting from a wrong policy followed by all governments and especially by Conservatives. To solely treat the symptoms would be like effecting a transfusion of blood in a seat of chronic infection. The way to attain a state of relative prosperity is to restore the purchasing power of the people destroyed by unsound methods applied to public administration.
The famous standard of living of the people is not the primary cause of this depression; it is rather to the wrong standard of living of those who have to do with high finance, and also t-o the enforcement of a poor financial policy that must be attributed, for the greater part, the present crisis. Justice demands that the people be protected against these parasites of the state, who have .placed fictitious values on their stocks, dividends or new issue of preferred shares. The tools of the state, such as the large corporations possessing no other rights but those granted by the authorities. Mr. Gladstone, the great Liberal leader of England, once told the workmen of a certain locality in the county of Chester, that the labour problem could not be solved like a mathematical problem, but that we must appeal to Christian feelings. There are, moreover, human economic means; if not of solving at least of improving the situation. Millions of unemployed workers are dependent not on theories or unworkable measures, but practical solutions. They have listened too long to these tiresome repetitions of theories, to these doleful distributors and will only be satisfied with regular work and equitable remuneration. All those who had work or are working to-day claim, rightly and justly, that they should be given continuous employment through a steadier functioning of industry. Large industrial and financial interests, during prosperous times, see that prices are maintained and that sufficient reserves are set aside to meet dividends and salaries in connection with the administration during periods of crises; but where is to be found in their reports, one item providing for the wages or part' of the wages of the workman who necessarily must join the ranks of the unemployed?
All this points to a real paradox: preventive measures are adopted against diseases, fire, hail, etc., but nothing of the kind exists againsts the ills of which millions of people suffer, as at present, owing to unemployment. The workmen, although forced to allow themselves to be doped by government assistance, protest and appeal to the authorities to apply the only solution possible: The necessary means to destroy unemployment at its outset.
We may provide for millions of days of work, but we shall not have found the antidote which is regularity of work in industries. This system, we must acknowledge, would perhaps not be, for the present, a complete cure, but it would provide a remedy which would relieve a great number of unemployed. But the idealists, together with certain people whose confidence reposes simply on these alibis, will perhaps reply by pointing out, as an excuse, the cycle of affairs, the feelings of the masses aroused, the lack of economy on the part of workers, etc., all such blinkers destined to cut off the light which would procure more genuine happiness in numerous homes which are today in want. It is regretful to note that this government has not, since the famous session of 1930, taken any steps to encourage industries to adopt such an attitude towards the unemployed.
The regularity of work, resulting from diversified and well managed production has already given convincing results to directors of companies who have taken the interest of their employees by putting into practice this motto, so truly human, of a manufacturer in France: work to earn and earn to give. Hon. members on this side who have taken part or purpose taking part in this debate do not feel we should be charged with obstructing. Actually we are fighting to maintain the rights of parliament. In his speech on Tuesday the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) said that the constitutionality of the measure now before us was settled by the vote last year. With that statement I totally disagree. True, parliament by that legislation did give certain rights and privileges to the executive, but may I add that the measure was opposed by practically every hon. member on this side of the house. The effect of the power given to the executive is that it may disregard any statute in Canada, and make any new regulation it sees fit. I do not believe the spirit which permeates Conservative minds is in sympathy with either the farmers or the unemployed. The government has another reason for maintaining this principle. If hon. members on this side concur in the resolution now before the house the principle will be maintained.
In my view the title of the bill was a misnomer, and a complete misrepresentation. It should have been entitled, "An act to delegate to the executive the power to grant additional privileges to financial interests, notwithstanding anything appearing in the statutes of Canada." That is the real purpose of the measure before the house, and to bear out my contention I shall trace the history of the government's action since the legislation of last year was passed.
One of the first orders in council had to do with the guarantee of $20,000,000 to the chartered banks of Canada to save them against any possible losses in connection with loans to the western wheat pool. That was a move to make sure that the big interests would not suffer.
The second order in council had to do with the prohibition of the export of gold, extending a special privilege to the banks whereby on application special export credits or privileges would be given. The effect of that order in council I should like to explain. Canadian bank notes had depreciated in value on the New York exchange: If a man went into a chartered bank in Canada and withdrew $500 in bank notes, took them to the United States and changed them into American money at the depreciated rate as it obtained early in the month of January, he would receive only $400 in American cash, thereby losing S100. If however the Canadian chartered banks could get a special privilege from the Minister of Finance to export some of their own gold reserve, they could,

Unemployment Continuance Act
by exporting $400 in gold, redeem in the United States clearing house, their own bank notes to the extent of $500. In that respect a special privilege was given to the banks.
The next order in council gave the banks the right to file with the Dominion government statements which were not according to the facts. In other words the banks could totally disregard the Bank Act of Canada and value their assets in any way that would be acceptable to the Minister of Finance. There, again, a special privilege was given to the big interests, with no regard whatever for farm or unemployment relief. Then, the other order in council, about which we heard so much a few evenings ago in the debate on the motion of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich), gave to the insurance companies of Canada the right to make a retroactive valuation of their stocks when on December 31, of this year, they filed their statements with the superintendent of insurance.
No one has condemned more than the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) wild speculation in Canada, and yet when one of the greatest financial houses in Canada-probably the greatest-finds itself in difficulty as a result of a wild orgy of speculation with trust funds which probably belonged to widows and orphans, all it had to do was to come to this Tory government and have an order in council passed allowing them to inflate the value of their stock holdings. Prominent newspapers have taken issue with the motion sponsored by the hon. member for Vegreville and with his statement that one of the insurance companies in Canada was, in effect, bankrupt. If the powers granted under the act of last year had not been exercised, and had the government not allowed this insurance company the right to make a retroactive valuation with respect to speculative stocks held, the statement of the hon. member would have been absolutely true. So much for the big interests.
Another very interesting order in council, a copy of which I hold in my hand, was passed. It authorized the government to expend $287,000 to increase the Royal Canadian Mounted Police by three hundred. Speaking in the house the other day the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce' (Mr. Stevens) said the reason for this increase was that an arrangement had been consummated with Alberta and the other western provinces whereby the Dominion government was taking over the policing of those provinces. It was not long before the inaccuracy of that statement was shown, because at the time of the
increase in the mounted police force there had been no negotiations with Alberta or with Manitoba. There was another reason for the increase of the mounted police entirely separate from the reason given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I can understand why the government is very much perturbed at the present time. The people of this country have been thoroughly fooled, and there are rumblings now in the back concessions-the people are getting dissatisfied. This government holds office by virtue of promises made. If members on the other side of the house had been honest during the campaign and had said to the industrialists, "If you vote for us we will put into effect policies which in two years will create conditions whereby the number of employees in your factories will be reduced by 200,000, and conditions will become so bad for you that you will be taking the greatest strain on your shoulders ever known in the history of this country," would they have received any votes in that quarter? They certainly would not. If the same gentlemen had said to the farmers, "Instead of blasting a way into the .markets of the world and selling your produce for you, after we have been in office two years and thoroughly put our policies into effect, the prices for your farm commodities will be the lowest known in your generation," would they have received the votes of the farmers? They certainly would not If our friends on the other side had said to the taxpayers, "After we get in office and have had a chance to demonstrate our policies, we will at the end of two years have a deficit of something over $225,000,000 and we will have put into effect every known method of taxation possible," would they have received any support from the taxpayers? They certainly would not. If instead of saying to the unemployed, "You vote for us and we will end unemployment or perish in the attempt; we will give work to every man who is willing to work," they had said honestly, "After being in office two years and thoroughly applying our policies, instead of 120,000 men out of work we will have
550,000	men on the streets," would they have received any votes from the unemployed? They certainly would not.
So these chickens are coming home to roost, and our hon. friends opposite are trying to avoid any further demonstration such as we had on parliament hill last week. And let me say a word with respect to that demonstration. I arrived at parliament hill at about two o'clock and was amazed to see guards at the gates armed to the teeth. 1 dodged out of the way of the armoured car

Unemployment Continuance Act
and kept clear of the cavalry. When I got to the main door I could see troops concealed in both directions. Why? Because some of these men who had 'been fooled by the wild promises of hon. gentlemen opposite were here as citizens of Canada to lay their just claims before the government of Canada. I went into the railway committee room and listened to the interview between the Prime Minister and the delegates representing these unfortunate unemployed men from practically every city in Canada. The Prime Minister had only twenty-five minutes of his valuable time to give them. He had plenty of time to satisfy his wounded vanity when that same day he attended before the committee that investigated the Gordon charges, but he had very little time, and very little patience either, for the unemployed. I listened to the presentation of their claims and I thought the delegates were very reasonable. These men were victims of a situation beyond their control, they were helpless, and they were looking to the Prime Minister to implement some of the promises he made to them when he was appealing for their votes in the campaign of 1930. But they got no satisfaction. I noticed among the delegates many members of the Canadian Legion. Being myself a member of the Legion, I took occasion to speak to these men. They said to me, "We fought for our country. We came down here to-day looking for bread, and we have received a stone from the Prime Minister. That is the gratitude we are getting from the man who appealed to us for our votes not quite two years ago."
Now, Mr. Speaker, when one sees what transpired the other day, and when one reads in this order in council that provision has been made for So,000 to purchase riot bombs and for S21.750 for new secret service men, one is forced to the conclusion that the effect of this power is to enable the executive to give the glad hand to the big interests and the mailed fist to the unemployed who are smarting under present conditions.
This afternoon I listened to our hon. friends across the way while they heckled and ridiculed the statements made by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), and I recalled that when those hon. gentlemen came down here after the election of 1930 they supported their leader enthusiastically; after the policies of the government had been in effect about a year and the results were beginning to show, and rumblings were being heard in the back concessions, the enthusiasm of our hon. friends opposite turned into dignified acquiescence; now when they are begin-

ning to feel the full weight of the effects of their policies they are giving the Prime Minister what you might call spineless subservience, because any man who at this time votes to delegate to the government all the rights of parliament must feel that from now on he is more or less of a rubber stamp. I do not know how otherwise he can justify his barren political existence. Our friends opposite are quite prepared at any time when the Prime Minister indicates how they should vote, to get up row by row and quiescently do his bidding.
Hear, hear.

"Hear, hear!" There is a typical disciple of the Prime Minister. He reminds me of the reference made the other day to the Prime Minister being like one of the sultans of old, that when he clapped his hands his janizaries jumped up to do his bidding. If hon. members across the way delegate all their power to the Prime Minister instead of parliament being a debating society, it just becomes the land of nod, and I would suggest that before the orders of the day are called they get their leader to tell them a bedtime story so that they may sleep all the afternoon. If their conscience is like their appendix, an inactive organ, they will have no trouble in sleeping soundly.
This motion, Mr. Speaker, is a challenge to responsible government. Never before have we had such a request made in any parliament that I know of. I only wish we had the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) on this side of the house. What a powerful oration he could deliver under these circumstances. I well remember when a few years ago I was sitting on the government side and the hon. gentleman-he was then in opposition-coined a new expression, and enunciated a new policy: he said that what we needed here was "red-blooded Canadianism." I recall vividly how he waxed eloquent on that theme; in fact he floated on the full tide of his own verbosity, so to speak. But fate plays strange pranks with the lives of men; the hon. gentleman now sits on the treasury benches and the responsibility of office has had a mellowing effect upon him. After he had been Minister of Railways for some few months he declared that what the Canadian people needed most of all was a tomato juice cocktail. His red-blooded Canadianism has turned into tomato juice at the present time. I think that change applies pretty generally throughout the ranks of our friends opposite.
Another hon. gentleman who has taken part in several debates is the member for South

Unemployment Continuance Act
Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), the present Minister of Justice. He turned a political somersault from the Liberal party and landed on the Tory benches-what might 'be termed an instance of economic determinism. That is what makes a man turn in the direction from which he hears the jingle of a cabinet minister's salary. But I do not think his efforts, or those of the Minister of Railways, who is also a former Liberal, have been appreciated, because in Guelph their own leader said that you can always depend upon a convert to make a mess of things. I think he spoke the truth, because the railway situation is worse than it ever has been 'before, while the Department of Justice is practically the only department this year requiring an additional vote in order to carry on.
The other day during the course of this debate the Minister of Railways had a very excellent opportunity to tell the people of Canada something about the complicated railway problems which confront the country at the present time, but he did not do that; instead he indulged in a wild discourse on Russia. I have something to say about Russia, because we have had a lot of speeches with regard to what is transpiring over there, and we have heard the Russian people condemned because a few of them happened to massacre the czar and his family. I hold no brief for the Russian people, but I do not choose to condemn 165,000,000 people because a few of them massacred their own crowned heads. As a direct result of this sort of talk we have practically prohibited all trade with Russia, and that has had a bad effect on the industrial life of Canada, particularly with regard to the agricultural implement plants in Brantford and Hamilton. Many men now out of work would have had employment if we had not indulged in such silly talk as we heard from the lips of the Minister of Railways the other day.
I know by the genial smile and twinkling eye of the Minister of Railways that he is a son of old Erin, and like all Irishmen he loves a fight. When the Irish cannot fight anyone else they fight among themselves. I know whereof I speak, .because my maternal grandfather came from Ireland, and when he landed here he still wore a bullet-proof vest, yet I think the Irish are among the most likeable and lovable people in the world. My grandfather, who came from Scotland, used to tell us that Mary Queen of Scots was taken to England from near where he lived, and executed; but he did not hold that against the English people at all; as a matter of fact on his farm in West Elgin he always had several
Englishmen working. Those men had no inferiority complex at all with regard to their own country; they thought, and perhaps rightly so, that you could not add to or take away from anything in British history, yet a few oenturies ago the British .people cut off the head of Charles I, although he was a quiet, lovable fellow. I do not hold that against the progeny of those British people at all. I heard the deputy speaker of this house (Mr. Lavergne) condemn the Russian? in a similar way, but some years ago his forebears in France rose in revolt against the thorough application of the caste system of the day, and I think if J had been there I would have been with them. They .beheaded Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, and knowing something of the fiery spirit of the deputy speaker I have no doubt he would have wielded an axe himself with considerable gusto if he had been in France at that time. Across the line our American friends at one time had a propensity for assassinating presidents, but I do not hold that against the American people. I do not think there is any other people in the world we would rather have on our southern boundary than the people of the United States. They even assassinated their great emancipator, Abraham Lincoln. I want to commend to hon. members across the way a few lines from that memorable address at Gettysburg, that great masterpiece of simple English.
Fourscore and seven years ago, our fathers brought forth on this continent a new nation, conceived in liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.
I have dealt, Mr. Speaker, with some of the civilized countries of the world, and I say that generally speaking we do not hold a grievance against any nation because in times past some group or other happened to assassinate some of the heads of that nation.
Now I should like to point out to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens)
[DOT] something that probably will be of interest to him. Some little time ago our Minister of Trade and Commerce was a soldier in the American army, and he went to the South Seas with a rifle and bayonet. I do not know why he needed the bayonet, because the cannibals of the South Sea islands were pretty elusive, and had to be shot on the run. But, as I say, he went to these islands with his rifle and bayonet. A few years later we find him as our Minister of Trade and Commerce, as a delegate from Canada, going to Honolulu to meet a delegate from our sister dominion of New Zealand in order to try to repair some

of the damage done by the Bennett eight cent tariff on butter. I do not think there was any warlike demonstration against him by the natives of that island because he had been there a few years before fighting their cannibalistic ancestors; in fact I believe they gave him a real welcome and decorated him with what is called the chain of peace. They even tell me that on the beach of Waikiki, where the natives dress like shredded wheat, they dedicated a song to our minister which was entitled " Honolulu Harry." So, Mr. Speaker, while that may sound rather ridiculous, it is no more ridiculous than the attack on Russia which has come from hon. gentlemen opposite.
Now I see my hon. friend the Minister of Justice is in his seat. The statement has been made that unemployment funds never have been used by this government for political purposes. I want to draw the attention of the minister to something that happened during the by-election in South Wellington. During the progress of that campaign there appeared in the newspapers an advertisement calling for tenders for the construction of a post office in the city of Guelph. Then on November 13, which was five days before the voting took place, this article appeared in the Guelph Daily Mercury:
Government Will Erect Fine Modern Structure On Quebec Street East Official Word from Ottawa Received by P. Kerwin, K.C., To-day Are Calling for Tenders Undertaking Will Provide Additional Work for City's Unemployed
Definite announcement was made to-day that Guelph will have a new post office and that it will be erected during the coming winter.
The official word was received by P. Kerwin, K.C., who is acting in the matter for the Department of Public Works and the Minister of Justice, the Hon. Hugh Guthrie, K.C., and the statement was also forwarded that tenders will be called for at once, 'with the closing date for the acceptance on these being set for December 10. The actual work on the building will be started just as soon as possible after a tender has been accepted.
Mr. Kerwin stated this morning that the prime object in the building of the new post office is to provide some relief for the unemployed men of this city and the assurance was given by officials that on the big job every possible bit of labour will be used. Men will be used to do the work instead of machinery in every possible case.
The site of the new post office is to be the property at present occupied by Daymond Bros., on Quebec street east, and the government, having taken over the ground, has notified the present occupants that they will be forced to vacate very soon.
Mr. Kerwin stated that he has been notified that the actual cost of the new post office, aside from the value of the land, will be from
fMr. Hepburn.]
one hundred to one hundred and twenty-five thousand dollars. A further announcement was made to the effect that the present post office is to be put into use as the headquarters of the local customs and excise officials.
While the definite announcement of the building of the new structure has only been made, the matter has been under consideration for some time. When inquiries were first made by the government as to what work in Canada could be proceeded with to relieve unemployment, the Hon. Hugh Guthrie, K.C., considered that a post office building was needed here, and he had investigations made as to the advisability of such a procedure. The result is that the work will be carried out.
Bearing in mind that this notice appeared in the local paper five days before voting took place in connection with that by-election in South Wellington, you can judge for yourself the effect it had among the unemployed. They were told by this notice that wherever possible men would be used to do the work instead of machinery. A few days ago I had an inquiry from Guelph asking why work had not been started on the post office. I put a question on the order paper, and I found that tenders were called for in accordance with the advertisement, the closing date being December 10. I asked if anyone had authority to issue a statement of that kind on behalf of the government, and here is the reply which was given:
No one has been authorized to make any statement on behalf of the government in respect to this matter.
Here is a case, Mr. Speaker, where the powers given this government could have been used, had the government so desired, to build a post office in Guelph without requiring a vote of this parliament, but the fact of the matter is that as yet the construction of a post office in that city has not been commenced. It looks to me as though first there was a conspiracy with the Department of Public Works to call for tenders, and that then whoever inspired this article, which was given out by the former partner of the present Minister of Justice, also conspired to fool the people of South Wellington. Yet they say the unemployment funds are not being used for political purposes.

I might also mention that the minister was there himself during the progress of the election; he had his private car spotted on the siding, but he folded his tent like the Arabs and faded quietly away when he found how the wind was blowing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I rise to correct an error
on the part of my hon. friend. He has charged that I was there and was taking part in that by-election. That statement is absolutely untrue. I went to Guelph to attend an Armistice day meeting, and left the same day to return to Ottawa. I did go up to vote. Had I been there I do not know that my hon. friend would have had so much to blow about.

Well, the fact stands out that we won the election, and I think the going will be pretty hard for the Minister of .Justice if he tries to get reelected himself. This indicates just what can be done if we set up a dictatorship in this country; but if we are going to have a dictator I should like to have a man of proven worth, not a man of extremes.
The Prime Minister states on the one hand that this is the best country in the world, while on the other he tries to justify his request for these unlimited powers on the ground that we are facing a great national crisis and that conditions are so bad that only such legislation as he asks for will meet the requirements of government at the present time. The right hon. gentleman has made extreme promises, and on top of all that he has said, "All these things I will do or perish in the attempt." These are the words of an extreme man. He says that he is feeding
300,000	people in Saskatchewan and he brags about it, and at the same time he is using the axe in Ottawa, so that while he is feeding all these people in Saskatchewan he is leaving others to starve here. He is a man of extremes, I say. I do not think he minds being referred to as a dictator; it rather tickles his inordinate vanity. It flatters him to be so described. Some people say that he is like Mussolini. I do not think the comparison is fair to Mussolini because after all Mussolini is accomplishing something: he is building up a national spirit in his own country- something the Prime Minister is not doing in Canada. Some of his admirers across the way
have referred to him as Napoleon. Well, there is only one similarity: Napoleon practised nepotism and put his relatives on the thrones of Europe. If the Prime Minister had another brotherdn-law, the Hon. Howard Ferguson's job in England as High Commissioner would not long be retained by that gentleman.
The Liberals of Ontario ought to be proud of their leader.

There is another interruption from the hon. member for South Essex-the Minister of Onions, someone says. But I can plead extenuating circumstances for the hon. gentleman because he comes from a riding in which there is located Jack Miner's famous wild goose sanctuary.
Pouliot told you that.

He is living among queer birds and he cannot get away from their influence. We have been interrupted so many times, Mr. Speaker, that I think it would be well to take up a collection and supply you with some insect powder to spray the hon. gentlemen with. The next time the hon. member interrupts us, let him have some of it. It will be justifiable homicide.
Mr. Speaker-
Sit down.

I want to say to the hon.
gentleman that one of the Prime Minister's passing thoughts would give him a headache.

I assure the hon. gentleman that if he had a headache it would get lonesome.
The only great autocrat in history that I can find, with whom I can fittingly compare the Prime Minister, is Nero. Nero had all the powers the Prime Minister is asking parliament to give him; yet he was a poor administrator. In fact, he ruined the civilization of his day. It is said that he fiddled while Rome burned, and we have the same situation in this country. The Prime Minister is trying one expedient after another, while debts and taxation are increasing and unemployment is getting worse, trade falling off, and commodity prices have fallen to the lowest level it has reached in the present decade.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: And you are doing the fiddling.

Hon. gentlemen opposite can sit with a smirk on their faces now, but they are humble when they get back to their own concessions. They are not so enthusiastic when they explain to their people the record

of this government. That brings to my mind an article I have here with reference to a speech delivered by the hon. member for Toronto Northeast (Mr. Baker). The hon. member was addressing Ward 9 Conservative Association in Toronto, with reference to the situation in this house-the hon. member for South Essex will have that spray gun turned on him if he does not keep quiet. This is what my hon. friend said:
"But, generally," he amended, "Mr. Bennett would stand it as long as he could, and then -would he go for them? And would they get it?"
Referring to the opposition.
Mr. Speaker-
Order.

I understood the hon.
member to say that he was quoting the member for Toronto Northwest.
Toronto Northeast.
Pardon me.

I do not blame any man for trying to get from under this kind of rubbish; I fully appreciate the hon. gentleman's feelings in this matter. According to the report, the hon. member for Toronto Northeast continued:
"He never lost his temper, mind you, but sometimes when his patience was stung to the limit he would start after them. Gentlemen, it was a treat of a lifetime to see the Hon. R. B. Bennett give it to them. And he generally closed the question. They didn't have much to say after he got through with them. For -there isn't a man in that house knows the ins and outs of every question the way he does. AVhen he summed up a situation there just wasn't anything left to say."
I have the honour to be the member for Toronto Northeast, and I should like to know when and where that was said.

The heading reads:
Ward Nine Tories held first meeting of the season.
Richard L. Baker, M.P.. and Coulter McLean, M.I'.P. are strong for leaders.
That appears under date October 15, 1931, in The Herald, North Toronto's Own Weekly.
I deny the accuracy of the statement.

Well, the only point I want to make in regard to this very illuminating and interesting and elevating address is with respect to the concluding sentence:
When he summed up a situation there just wasn't anything left to say.

That applies very well to hon. members across the way, because they dare not say anything after the Prime Minister has summed up a situation. I want to say to the right hon. gentleman that we on this side are not going to be bullied or browbeaten or intimidated by him or any other hon. gentleman there.
Now, Mr. Speaker, a further reason why I do not like to delegate all these powers to the present executive is that I do not think their policies are applicable to the best interests of the country. After all, this country has an ever-increasing exportable surplus, and its future development and prosperity depend upon an expansive trade policy and not a policy of trade restriction such as is in force at the present time. The government's policy is becoming more drastic all the time and the only thing left for the Prime Minister to do is to order the guns of Quebec to fire on trading vessels coming up the St. Lawrence, or to bring back our wandering navy and station it at Vancouver island to attack any trading ships coming up the Pacific coast. Probably hon. members opposite think I am a little bit bitter in my condemnation of the government.
Oh, no.

But let me say that in the back concessions the people are actually suffering to-day as a result of the application of the present government's policies. There is real suffering among these people and I sympathize with them; and I lay the whole blame on the Tory element, not only in this country but in every other country. But we in this country particularly had a glaring example of the application of Tory policies at the special session of the Canadian parliament held in September, 1930. In 1928 we had in this house the report of an economic commission which had investigated conditions in our sister dominion of Australia. There they were just a little ahead of us in the application of the same kind of policy we have adopted. They put into effect a forty per cent tariff, thus serving to stimulate falsely the industries of that country, and increasing the cost of production to the basic producer. The farmer of Australia, the real wealth-producer, could not get a corresponding increase in price for his wheat or butter or anything he had to sell, although he had to pay more in cost of production. So that in the great struggle for world markets the basic producers were actually put out of business there. Industries falsely bolstered up could not be maintained, with the result that there was chaos; and then

Unemployment Continuance Act
the basic producers, who were suffering most of all as a result of that policy, applied to the government. The government in the second of the three stages leading to bankruptcy started to subsidize. The first stage was high tariffs; the second stage was subsidies. Then when the people started to feed out of the public treasury they found that they could not stand the taxation any longer, and the whole financial structure of Australia collapsed, and collapsed as a result of the application of the very same policies which were put into effect by hon. gentlemen opposite in the special session of 1930.
In the United States we had a very similar situation. Notwithstanding the glaring example of what had occurred in Australia, President Hoover, for his own aggrandizement, went up and down the country promising the basic producers increased prices for their products if they would but vote for his high tariff policy. He put that policy into effect, increased the tariff on 1,100 articles of trade, but that did not help the basic producers of that country in any way. The basic producer is not getting any more for his products, which are sold in competition with other countries. The wheat grower is not getting any more, the cotton grower is not getting any more, the dairy producer is not getting any more for his products, but the basic producer did lose in this respect, that he had to stand increased production costs, and on the other hand the markets in which he might have sold his products were closed to him as the result of the policies put into effect by President Hoover. There was the second stage.
After high tariffs, you found subsidies applied. Then the government was confronted with the people clamouring for President Hoover to redeem his promises, and the only thing left to do was for President Hoover to appropriate money out of the treasury, which he did to the amount of $500,000,000, and he put this huge revolving farm loan fund into the hands of a board created by himself. This board tried by unsound economic measures to buy wheat off the market, to buy dairy products off the market, and to buy cotton off the market, in order falsely to stimulate the price. But that did not help the basic producers. After this $500,000,000 revolving fund had been appropriated by President Hoover, the basic producers, to their disillusionment, saw the prices of their products go to the lowest level known in the history of the United States, and now these same producers have to stand additional taxation to meet the deficit created by such a policy. There in the United States, as well
as in Australia, you see first of all high tariffs, then the demand for subsidies, then a huge deficit, and' in the end there will be bankruptcy over there unless their policy is changed. So I say that we had these examples before us of a thorough application of such a policy in the United States and of a thorough application of such a policy in Australia, and yet hon. gentlemen opposite, for their own aggrandizement, adopted this false doctrine which they knew was not applicable to the needs of this country. The events which have transpired since they adopted such a policy have proved beyond a shadow of a doubt that what I say is absolutely true.
Are we fundamentally tackling any of the great problems before us in this country? Certainly not. We are simply resorting to expedients. Is there any justification for a five cent bonus on wheat? It is just a sop to the western wheat farmers. The tariff policy of this government has cost the western wheat farmers $200,000,000, yearly, and then as a sop the government throw to them a bonus of five cents a bushel on wheat.
We had a debate on wool in this house the other day, and hon. gentlemen opposite supported a tariff on wool. That is an unsound policy, because we are now exporting more of the wool produced in Canada than our domestic market can consume.

I would like in a few words and in a simple manner to sum up what has been said in this debate. I do not intend to guillotine any crowned heads, to shoot any cannibals in the back, or to eat any Russians. The question raised by the opposition is a constitutional issue. It is whether parliament shall be supreme over the expenditure of public moneys, or whether the governor in council shall be given while parliament is sitting the powers which the government possesses during the recess, powers which expired on March 1, nearly a month after the opening of parliament, and which the government seeks to have continued until May 1.

With the object of recalling the matter to mind and in order to convince the government the return to the land is a sound policy, that the expenditure of millions in furtherance of the return to the land is a good investment for the country, I will quote a few observations made by a Catholic priest who was a leader in the agricultural settlement of the country.

I am glad to offer my congratulations to hon. members on both sides of the house who are observing this as a national day of celebration. St. Patrick was a good saint and a great protector; I am told he belonged to no party at all and never entered politics, and therefore he is always blessing good Irishmen all over the world.
Speaking of St. Patrick reminds me of a man in provincial politics in Quebec of whom we have heard a good deal in the last week or so. I refer to Hon. Mr. Dillon, who was in charge of a bill which passed the Quebec legislature last session. I see my good friend from Compton (Mr. Gobeil) in the house. He made quite a long speech yesterday about Mr. Dillon and his bill, but that must be a sound law-
Oh, oh.

Just a moment. I also see my good friend from Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Moore), who is also a worthy Irishman. This must have been good law, because it was introduced by an Irishman, and when it left the legislative assembly and went to the council it was sponsored by Hon. Mr. Bryson, another able Irishman, and was seconded by Mr. Kelly, still another reputable Irishman. That law has helped many elected candidates, and they were not all Liberals. I know that
for one it helped Mr. Bertrand, who is now a Conservative member of the legislative assembly for Saint-Sauveur. His election was contested and because of that law he now represents that constituency. Ask Mr. Bertrand if he does not bless that law to-day; he knows it gave him the chance to sit in the provincial house as a Conservative member. To meet the argument advanced by my hon. friend opposite let us imagine that the Liberal party, after the last dominion election had contested one hundred seats in the house. Of course that is absurd, but by making a comparison it is easier to understand the fact. It would have been an intolerable thing if we had taken that action; perhaps an order in council would have been passed by the present government, declaring the petition null and void. But we saw the spectacle in the province of Quebec of 55 seats being contested, some of them having been won by majorities ranging from 500 to 1,500, as was the case in my own county of St. Henri. Of course when we look at a thing through a binocular it always seems greater than when we look at it through a microscope; in the latter case it seems very small.
During the course of this debate we have heard many things about the province of Quebec. As members of parliament we should do our best to foster a proper appreciation of the provinces from which we come. What is the use of criticizing the Liberal administration in Quebec because it is a Liberal one? Why suggest that the people were bluffed in the last election in that province? The people were not fooled, they were not bluffed; you cannot fill them up as though they were bottles. The Liberal party in that province were returned by a vote of the majority of the people, and any stranger, viewing the situation impartially, will agree that the people in that province were right. Where is my proof in support of my contention that the people of Quebec were right in returning the Liberal government to power? It is to be found in the report of the Dominion Director of Unemployment Relief, March 1, 1932, published by this government. This report gives an accounting of the appropriations and disbursements throughout Canada under the act. I do not find, according to the report, that my province has come to Ottawa and asked for any advances, but I do find that the province of Manitoba asked for three and three quarter millions, Saskatchewan almost seventeen millions, and Alberta four and a half millions. And what about the province of Ontario- a wealthy province forming, along with the province of Quebec, the cornerstone

of the Dominion of Canada? It is true that Ontario asked for a small amount, but just the same that province did ask for $190,364,74. Then British Columbia, on the verge of bankruptcy, gets an advance of $5,664,366.19. Altogether, we find that over $31,000,000 has been advanced to five of the provinces; but I see nowhere any mention of the province of Quebec. Now I do not say this in order to belittle any of the other provinces of Canada; not at all. My sentiments are too broad for that. I know that the nine provinces of Canada are the nine jewels in the crown of confederation, and each part of the dominion should be willing, if necessary, to come to the assistance of the rest. On the other hand, I think that my contention is borne out by the figures disclosed in this report, for they show the condition of the province of Quebec, the first settled land in this dominion. My province, I claim, still leads the dominion. I am proud of that province, and when I say so I am speaking on behalf not only of the Liberals of Quebec but of all the people who so strongly supported the government of Premier Taschereau in the last provincial election.
The province of Quebec, we are told, had a deficit of $10,000,000. As everyone knows, we were obliged to contribute our share under the unemployment relief scheme. For every dollar advanced, for provincial works, Quebec was obliged to pay its share on a fifty per cent basis, and for municipal works, Quebec was paying between thirty-five and forty-five per cent. We were obliged to take money from the treasury of Quebec to contribute to such work as was done. Perhaps other provinces were not on a financial basis strong enough to meet current liabilities, but Quebec was ready to meet hers, from her surpluses. But at that very moment she was obliged to contribute millions towards works carried on in the metropolis of Canada. It is not surprising, therefore, that the treasury of the province should be depleted after helping to meet the exigencies of the federal government. But let me say that before the first of May the banks will be reimbursed that $10000,000, for the credit of the province of Quebec is still unimpaired in Canada, in England, and in every other country of the world, and Quebec will come back with flying colours. That province will balance its budget and will go ahead and prosper, to the advantage of the farmers and the people of the cities.
I have looked through this report very carefully, and it is astonishing to see the amount of money that has been spent under the Unemployment Relief Act. I may say quite

frankly that when the bill was introduced last year I realized that the situation was desperate. When the Liberal government was in power there were signs of the tornado that was about to strike us. Anyone could see the clouds hanging over us, and the Liberal government foretold a tremendous storm. Our opponents did not agree with us, but the storm came just the same and we are in the midst of it now.
I should have liked to see this bill drafted differently. Does any business man in this house imagine for a moment that he would confer upon his manager or upon any other person in his firm or industry such wide powers as were given to the government under this act? Not at all. Not at all. Parliament must retain control over the expenditure and over the mandate given to the government so that we may hold the government to account and see that our ministers do not engage in risky undertakings. The government are asking that the powers conferred under the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act of 1931 be extended for a further two months. It is true that the government has presented a report on .the work that has been done under this act, but why does not the government ask parliament to vote a specific amount? If it did that, I would be the first to support it. Navigation will be opening up at Montreal within two months. I see on -page 19 of the report on the administration of the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, schedule 18, that there has been spent by the Dominion government, as its share, in the city of Montreal for public works $1,200,000, but I contend, Mr. Speaker, that the money should not have been spent in the way it was. I am not here to give advice, for I know that any advice coming from the opposition will not be listened to by the government, that it will have no more chance than a cat jumping in an alley. But if the money had been spent on improvements to the Montreal harbour, for instance, not only would it have given work to the labouring people of Montreal, but work would have been done that would have been of benefit to the city and to this whole country for the next ten or fifteen years. Sheds, for instance, might have been built and new construction of various kinds which would have supplied the port's requirements for the next ten or fifteen years. The unemployed in Montreal would be glad to work with a pick and shovel on this work. I contend that that would have been a much better way to spend the money, because not only would work have been provided but public works of value would have been constructed which would

serve this country for a considerable number of years to come. The government might have built a new custom house, for instance, at Montreal. A foundation was laid for such a building nearly fifteen years ago 'by a former Conservative government, under Sir Robert Borden. This foundation on McGill street cost approximately $1,000,000, but nothing further was done with regard to it. If work had been proceeded with on that project, we would to-day have a new federal building in the city of Montreal which would have served the needs of the city for perhaps twenty-five years hence, and at the same time work would have been provided for the unemployed. But I humbly submit that at present the money is being spent in a way that is not of benefit to Canada, and if this crisis continues, and if the treasury remains empty of revenue, the government will 'be obliged to increase taxation. They will have to borrow money and they will not be able to say to the people: Look at the public works that we have built with the money voted for unemployment relief. It would have been far better to construct public buildings, dredge rivers, and make harbour improvements, providing for the needs of the future as well as looking after the present.
I read in a Montreal paper a few months ago-if I am wrong I shall be glad to be corrected-that the chairman of the Montreal harbour commission had urged the building of a wharf and shed at Windmill Point at Montreal. This project would have provided work for a very considerable number of men and would have been of benefit to the Marine department and to Canada as a whole. But nothing was done. If that project had been gone on with, you would not see, 30,000 unemployed walking the streets of Montreal today. Money voted for unemployment relief and to be spent in the city of Montreal should have been spent in the harbour of Montreal, in the construction of improvements.
In distributing the money to municipalities, I contend that the government is relinquishing too much of the control over the funds voted by parliament. In the city of Montreal, for instance, more was expended in expropriation proceedings than on public works undertaken for the benefit of the unemployed. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment which this government has proposed will be withdrawn because I humbly submit that a constitutional issue is involved. The control of public moneys should not be taken out of the hands of parliament.
I heard the learned speech the other day of my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and
Commerce (Mr. Stevens). He argued that it was impossible to spend a definite amount without asking parliament to vote it, and that if it was not voted the Auditor General would scrutinize the item very closely to see that it was devoted to the purpose designated by the house. That is the very principle that I am advocating, that parliament should have control over the moneys it votes. But today we do not know where we are going. Are we going to spend fifteen or twenty or fifty million dollars during the next few months for the relief of unemployment? Nobody knows. But if the government would ask this house to vote a definite sum,, say fifty or sixty million dollars, if needed, that would be in accordance with constitutional practice and in accordance with the principle of the voting of supplies by parliament which has always prevailed in this country.
I hope that I have not delayed the house too long, Mr. Speaker, but what I have said I have said sincerely, presenting my view as to the issue involved, and speaking also in the interests not only of the city of Montreal but also of my beloved province of Quebec, which in common with the other provinces of this dominion is vitally concerned in the prosperity and welfare of our country.

In rising to make a few observations on the resolution before the house, I wish to be as fair as I can and to present the view which is taken by hon. members on this side of the house.
At the outset there is one question that I should like (to ask. If the government were very anxious to bring in this measure in time to have the amendment made before the first of March, why did they not introduce it earlier in the session? The speech from the throne was disposed of in a couple of days and there was no reason in (the world why the government could not have introduced this measure and had the act amended before it lapsed. Our friends, however, chose to sit back quietly, do nothing in connection with the situation, and allow the act to lapse. Then, after it was dead, they came to parliament and asked for an amendment to what has been termed a dead statute. I do not think our hon. friends opposite or the country at large can take any objection to the criticism that has been offered by this side of the house, because it has been made clear from the first that the Liberal party are perfectly willing to vote the supply necessary to carry on any undertakings the government may have on hand or any new ones on which they may wish to embark. It was made quite plain by the

leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) 'that if a supply bill were brought in to take care of any emergency that might arise, it would be put through the house in the course of a few hours and then the government could bring in a new bill which they could frame at their leisure, without attempting to rush through a bill to amend an act which, as has been pointed out, is defunct and no longer capable of amendment.
