It is true that at that time an appropriation might have been voted, and it was very largely the burden of the complaint of some hon. members that that was not done, but I invite hon. gentlemen to consider this, that when an appropriation is passed the purpose for which it is to be used must be specified, and the Auditor General and other officers of the crown in scrutinizing expenditures under such an appropriation always keep the government very closely to the purpose specified in such a vote.
If there has been advanced from any part of the house one argument which condemns more strongly than any other the action of the government in proposing this amendment to the act, it is the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He says positively that if they bring in a supply bill, then the country is going to know where every dollar of that money has gone. If they bring in an amendment to the act, then the government can do almost anything they want and the Auditor General has not the power to scrutinize that he would have if a specified1 sum were voted.

I am quite sure my hon. friend does not wish to misrepresent my statement. If he will refer to the remarks which I made on 'that occasion, and part of which he has just quoted, he will note that I was referring to conditions that -could not possibly have been foreseen or provided for, and therefore an appropriation which must specify what it is for, -could not be used for unforeseen cir-

cumstanees which might arise under these emergent -conditions, particularly the drought conditions of the west.

My hon. friend's argument would hold good if the house were not in session; but the government must know the commitments they have made up to the present time; they must have a fairly good estimate of what is needed for the different provinces, and they could have brought in a supply bill sufficiently large to take care of any emergency that might arise within the next two months. That supply bill could have been passed by the house and then the Auditor General could have been in a position to check up and see where every dollar of the money went. The hon. member for St. Henri (Mr. Mercier) has referred to the report which has been submitted to the house. What does that report show? Do we get any itemized expenditure in it? We do not. All we get is a statement showing lump sums that were approved by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), one sum for this province and another for that. Those appropriations were approved and the government gave the municipality or the provincial government authority to go ahead and carry out the relief works at a specified amount. Nobody knows whether those projects cost too much or not, or what was done for the amount stated, or how the money was really expended. I do not wish to be harsh, but if when the former Liberal government was in power my hon. friends opposite had had half the chance that we on this side have had, I know the criticism they would have offered. As I said before, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has condemned this course of asking for a blank cheque more strongly than any member on this side has been able to condemn it.
If they are given a blank cheque and this wide power in regard to the provision for peace, order and good government, they may do anything. We might have a merger of all the banks in Canada; we might have a merger of the great railway systems; we might have the deep waterway scheme put through in this country by order in council, and we know how divided public opinion is on the question. We know the attitude which is being taken in the great province of Quebec; they are prepared to carry the matter to the seat of the throne rather than give away their rights. Therefore, to give this blank cheque and this wide power of legislation to the government at this time, is going a step too far. The situation should be dealt with as it arises; our friends opposite should

now know pretty nearly what they want; they should bring in a new bill and allow the house to debate it, without asking for a blank cheque at this stage of the game.
They say that we have made no worthwhile suggestions. It has been pointed out by the speakers to-night that the leader of the opposition has on different occasions indicated that the appointment of an independent commission in each province is the proper manner of handling the situation. This is the people's money. One of the regulations approved by the Minister of Labour under the statute that was passed is as follows:
All agreements with provincial and municipal authorities shall contain a provision to the effect that all persons employed on the works or undertakings referred to herein shall be residents of Canada, and in no case shall discrimination be made or permitted in the employment of or in the granting of direct relief to any British subjects by reason of their political affiliation, race or religious views.
This was to be a fair deal to the country as a whole. We have heard representatives from different provinces state that this principle has not been followed. I am not going to complain in regard to Prince Edward Island; I think the work was handled there as well as in any other province, but a new Conservative government had just come into power; their friends were very hungry for government jobs, and there is no doubt in the world that they pressed that government very hard. We had complaints by the score from people who said that no one need apply unless he was of the right political stripe. I do not know whether or not that is true, but I do know that we have had complaints that the money did not go to the men who needed it, that for some reason or another those moneys in many cases did not reach their proper destination-that is, the man out of work. A large amount of the money spent went to people who did not need it, to people who could afford to buy motor trucks, to merchants, to contractors and to speculators who were able to grab a large proportion of the money. Those people received the benefit rather than the men who were really in need of assistance. No wonder the public press and the people in general condemn this measure. I think it was "Alfalfa Bill" Murray, or Senator Bill Murray, of the United States who said that people do not exist for government, but that the government exists for the benefit of the people. Our hon. friends opposite seem to think that the people exist for the government, and we find them endeavouring to control everything in the way of expenditures to suit themselves.
Turning to the public press for expressions in this connection we find the following in the Financial Post;
It must be obvious to everyone that the proposed plan for carrying on relief work in the same way as last season does not commend itself to the public generally.
When we see such papers as the Financial Post, publications which have made a study of the plan, condemn it and make publicly the statement that the procedure is too expensive, I think it is time for the government to call a halt and take into consideration some of the suggestions put forward by the press and by hon. members in this house.
The Financial Post of January 30, 1931, states that $10 has been added to the public debt of Canada for every day's work given to the unemployed. The figures reveal waste and prove that the plan is unsound, that it is calculated to strain the credit of municipalities and provinces, and is loading them up with debts that they would not otherwise assume. That is the view of the Financial Post. In the same issue I find the following statement:
In other words, it cost the state not more than $20 per head to carry the unemployed under direct relief, and $210 per head to give 332,000 people 22 days work each in the year. The expense of the relief work was at least ten times greater than that of direct relief. The figures for this year will run about the same.
That is the astounding statement contained in the Financial Post, a publication which has gone into this matter thoroughly and has attempted to show to the public that the giving of relief has not been economically handled. The article in the Financial Post goes on to say:
A relief problem of 350,000 unemployed, therefore, can be met by direct relief for $7,000,000; by indirect relief (22 days work apiece), $70,000,000.
An analysis has been made by that publication to show that some $60,000,000 has been thrown away in an attempt to carry out the relief plan adopted last year by my hon. friends opposite.
Concerning the question whether or not the provinces are able to carry on, a great deal has been published in the public press. Mr. C. A. Bogert, general manager of the Dominion bank, stated at the annual meeting of that institution that Canada is now borrowing $6 for each SI she is repaying. Referring to the public debt of Canada he said:
The Dominion government during the past few years had reduced the public debt approximately 11 per cent from its peak, but this again was more than wiped out in the past few weeks by the national service loan.

That is a very strong statement coming from a man who holds the position of general manager in one of our greatest banks. Hon. members must realize that we cannot go on rolling up debts in the municipal, provincial and dominion governments, because there is a limit to credit. The time would soon come when even this Dominion of Canada would not be in a position to borrow enough money to keep going. There is no use misleading the people regarding these grants, because down in our little province of Prince Edward Island we know that in the past few years we received fair treatment from the federal Department of Public Works. Last year, however, when the dominion government gave $125,000 to that province for unemployment the contribution was heralded throughout the press, and statements were made about the wonderful help the federal government was giving. May I point out that on the one hand this government is withholding hundreds of thousands of dollars from Prince Edward Island, and on the other hand it is making a contribution of $125,000 for the relief of the unemployed.
Let us survey the situation. We find that the amount voted for public works in the province of Prince Edward Island for the year 1928 was $339,800. In 1929, the sum of $229,800 was voted. What do we find in the estimates for 1932? There are only two items, totalling $8,000. Yet, under a Liberal government in 1929 the province of Prince Edward Island received $339,800. Although our hon. friends opposite are spending money for the relief of the unemployed, they are at the same time allowing the public works of this dominion to run down. Public works in the province of Prince Edward Island will fall into a state of decay; the amount stipulated in the estimates for this year is not sufficient to keep them in repair. True, the sum of $50,000 is set aside for harbours and rivers. That sum, however, is voted every year, and is used only in cases of emergency where trouble may develop after a storm, and repair work may be necessary.
Let us consider dredging in the maritimes. In the year 1929, the sum of $540,000 was set aside for that purpose, and of that sum $60,000 or $70,000 was spent in the constituency I have the honour to represent. We find that for 1931-32 the amount was only $235,500, indicating a reduction in that one item of $304,500.
The Conservative governments apparently did more for the hon. member than the Liberal governments did for us.

I think the records show that the country was well cared for by the Liberal government. During the last election campaign the Conservative candidates were telling about the wonderful things they were going to do when their party came into power, so far, none of their promises have been fulfilled. They promised to find a market for our products. They went up and down the country telling the people to look at their milk cheques. I ask my hon. friends to-night to look at their milk cheques, and not only their milk cheques but all other cheques for farm produce. Look at the cheques they receive from the sale of their potatoes, their poultry, their pork, their beef, their grain. I ask my hon. friends what has happened to those silver-lined promises they handed out so freely during the election campaign.
In the few moments I have at my disposal before eleven o'clock I wish to make an appeal to this government on behalf of the potato growers in Prince Edward Island. Millions of dollars have been voted in this house for the benefit of other provinces. My hon. friend from the province of Quebec who preceded me told us that within the last year about $32,000,090 had been voted to the different provinces to take care of unemployment and farm relief. If hon. members would take the time to search the records from confederation up to the present they would not find one dollar voted for the relief of farmers in Prince Edward Island. To-day those farmers are in a worse position than they have been at any time since confederation. In western Canada the farmers are blessed with a fertile soil, and about all they need do is put in their crop; then if there is anything like a good growing season they are assured of a bountiful harvest. In short, the only essential thing is seed. But in Prince Edward Island we need not only seed, but something that is equally essential-fertilizer. For the past two years our farmers down there have been in a most unfortunate position. Last fall the potato association shipped large quantities of potatoes into the United States on the understanding that they would be sold when the market opened up this spring. They had to pay the duty and freight and storage charges, and now the prospects are that they will get scarcely anything in return. I see my friends from Prince Edward Island on the other side and I know they will agree with every word I say. To-day our farmers need some cash assistance to help them buy their fertilizer for this year's crop. They cannot get that fertilizer on credit because it is a cash article. The banks are carrying the

Unemployment Continuance Act
farmer's notes for the fertilizer purchased last year and they decline to make any further advances for this year's requirements. I appeal to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) -and if the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. M eir) were in his seat I would make the same appeal to him; I appeal to them to have a survey made of the situation. It can be easily done through the provincial government or the Potato Growers' Association, either of whom, I know, would verify the statements I am now making. I think the provincial government and the association would be well-advised to put in a claim for $500,000 to enable the farmers to get their fertilizer this year. If this appropriation were made it would be greatly appreciated by our farmers on the island, and would be only doing justice to the province in view of the millions of dollars that have been voted to the farmers of the western provinces. Our friends opposite were going to blast a way into the markets of the world, but they have not been able to blast out of the way even that little insect, the potato bug, and so get removal of the British embargo against our potatoes. I believe unless our farmers can get an outside market for their potatoes they will have to discontinue potato growing altogether.
The question of subsidies has also been agitating our people in Prince Edward Island. In the election of 1930 they were told that if the Conservative party came into power the Duncan report would be fully implemented; but this government has not shown the slightest disposition to redeem that promise. I know that the Conservative campaign literature circulated throughout the province at that time was very definite in promising that if the party was successful they would supplement the treasury of Prince Edward Island by a subsidy of $700,000. I see the premier of the province in his budget speech states that the provincial debt in 1910 was $877,756, that by 1920 it had grown to $1,176,264, and that at the end of 1931 it had pyramided to 83,342,241

or an increase in the last eleven years of $2,165,817. It took fifty years from confederation up to 1910 to bring the debt of the island up to less than a million dollars, yet in the decade from 1920 it has, as stated by the Premier, reached a total of over three million dollars. From this it will be apparent to every hon. member how necessary it is that the province should have an increased subsidy. The premier paid a wonderful tribute to the Liberal party in his budget speech. He said in effect that the Liberal government under Mr. Mackenzie King had increased the subsidy by $125,000. When asked by the
opposition if anything had been done with regard to getting a further increase, he said, "No, now is not the time to go to Ottawa to ask for an increased subsidy. It will be years before we can get any increase." In that statement he unconsciously paid a fine tribute to the Liberal government. In effect he said: We got $125,000 -under the Liberal government, we have not been able to get a cent since, and we shall have to wait until the Liberal party gets back to power before we can expect a further increase in our subsidy.
